data.title: Which human ageing phenotypes are causally reversible by mTOR modulation — and is it the same mechanism in each tissue?
data.evidence_stands_at: Clinical outcome in humans — mixed and partly negative
data.gap: Does rapamycin extend human lifespan is not a testable question on any useful timescale, and treating it as the goal has let a set of much sharper questions go unasked. Immune ageing, sarcopenia, metabolic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, fibrosis and stem-cell exhaustion are separate phenotypes with separate readouts, and there is no reason to assume one drug reaches them all or reaches them by the same route.
data.gap_beginner: Asking whether a drug makes people live longer cannot be answered in any reasonable amount of time, and aiming at it has crowded out better questions. Ageing is not one thing: the immune system, muscle, metabolism and the brain each age in their own way, and a drug might reach some of them and miss others entirely.
data.changed_since_written: The human results that have arrived are tissue-specific and they do not agree with each other. A phase 3 trial of low-dose TORC1 inhibition (RTB101) did engage its target - it upregulated interferon-induced antiviral genes in the blood in both the phase 2b and phase 3 trials - yet it did not reduce clinically symptomatic respiratory illness in older adults (Mannick, Lancet Healthy Longev 2021, PMID 33977284); the authors attribute the miss to a changed symptom-based endpoint and a healthier population, not to a failure to hit the target. In the brain the problem was the opposite: one 2025 trial found rapamycin undetectable in cerebrospinal fluid, with no cognitive change, while CSF p-tau181, GFAP and neurofilament light rose (Gonzales, Commun Med 2025, PMID 40394335), and a second found no change in cerebral glucose metabolism on FDG-PET (Svensson, medRxiv 2025, preprint); brain exposure was never demonstrated. In muscle, 48 weeks of intermittent dosing raised lean mass in women rather than lowering it (Moel, Aging 2025, PMID 40188830). Same drug, three tissues, three different kinds of answer. A fourth tissue has since reported in the other direction: in six men aged 70 to 76 given 1 mg rapamycin daily for eight weeks, transmitral blood flow, peak flow rate and maximal blood acceleration on cardiac MRI improved significantly, as did cutaneous endothelial function on laser-Doppler flowmetry (Moody, GeroScience 2025, PMID 40971115). The design carries almost no weight on its own - open-label, no placebo arm, n=6, men only - but it is the first human functional phenotype to move favourably under mTOR inhibition, rather than a marker or a null.
data.still_open: Which phenotypes replicate under placebo control, and whether the mechanism is shared. The cardiovascular signal (Moody, GeroScience 2025, PMID 40971115) is the only candidate so far and it is unreplicated, open-label and male-only, so the question has moved from no candidate phenotype to one that a powered trial has yet to confirm. The failures do not all have the same shape, and that distinction matters: the brain trials failed at exposure - the drug was not shown to reach the tissue at all - whereas the immune trial reached its target and still missed its clinical endpoint. So two separate questions remain open: what counts as demonstrated mTOR target engagement in a given human tissue (the brain question), and which clinical endpoint and which responders a trial should use once engagement is in hand (the immune question).
data.why_it_matters: It replaces one unanswerable question with several answerable ones. For the brain trials it reframes the negatives as an exposure problem - the drug was never shown to reach the brain - so those results do not refute the biology. That reading does not stretch to every negative trial, though: the immune trial did engage its target and still missed its clinical endpoint, so there the open issue is the endpoint and the responder population, not exposure.
data.how_to_test: Phenotype-first rather than drug-first. Pick one tissue where target engagement can be demonstrated directly — skin, blood or muscle, all biopsiable — fix the regimen against a measured pharmacodynamic endpoint in that tissue, and only then test a functional outcome. Run the same design across tissues and compare the pharmacodynamic signature that accompanies benefit in each. Whether the signature is shared answers the mechanism half.
